name: Single Responsibility Principle
intent: Give each module one reason to change, meaning one actor or stakeholder whose needs drive its edits, so that a change requested by one group cannot break the behaviour another group depends on.
scenario: A payroll report class calculates pay, formats it as a file and saves it. In one quarter finance changes a tax rule, operations asks for a new output format and IT moves the storage to a database. All three edits land in the same class, and each one risks breaking the other two. The team compares the single class, a split by reason to change, and an over-split design with a class for every step.
problem: The principle is usually repeated as "a class should do one thing", and that wording misleads in both directions. Read literally, almost anything does several things, so teams either ignore it or split code into dozens of tiny classes that nobody can follow. The useful reading is about change: a module should have one reason to change, one actor whose needs drive its edits. When finance and operations share a class, a tax fix can break the report layout, both teams must coordinate every release, and the tests for unrelated behaviour have to run again for every edit.

howItWorks.title: Find the reasons to change
howItWorks.text: List who can ask for a change to this code: finance for pay rules, operations for output formats, IT for storage. Each of those groups is an actor, and the code that serves one actor changes for that actor's reasons. Robert Martin's wording is that a module should be responsible to one, and only one, actor. The count of methods and the count of verbs in a description are not the test.

howItWorks.title: Keep what changes together, together
howItWorks.text: Group the code that one actor drives into one module, even if it does several steps. Overtime, tax and bonus rules all change for finance and usually change in the same release, so they can live in one calculator. Splitting them into three classes would not give three reasons to change, it would spread one reason over three files.

howItWorks.title: Separate what changes for different reasons
howItWorks.text: Pull apart code that serves different actors: the pay calculation, the report layout and the storage code. A tax change then edits the calculator and nothing else, and only the calculator and the code that calls it need re-testing: no formatting or storage behaviour sits in the edited class. Calls between the parts stay simple: a thin coordinator asks the calculator for numbers, the formatter for text and the store to save it.

howItWorks.title: Check the cost of the split
howItWorks.text: Every split adds a boundary: a new name, a call between modules and a place to look when you follow the flow. Splitting past the actors gives one reason to change spread over several classes, so a single tax change edits three files and following one report run means reading sixteen. The principle has been over-applied when one change touches many classes, or when you cannot say who owns a class.

howItWorks.title: Re-draw the line when the actors change
howItWorks.text: The boundaries follow people and teams, not the code. If finance and operations merge, or one team takes over storage, the split can be merged back. If a class starts receiving requests from a second group, that is the signal to separate it. Treat the design as a response to the changes you actually see, not to every change you can imagine.

pros: A request from one team edits code that only that team cares about
Less unrelated behaviour to re-verify after each change
Teams can release changes to their own part without coordinating with others
Small, focused classes are easier to name, read and test on their own
cons: More classes and more calls between them, so following the flow takes more reading
The right split depends on knowing who the actors are, which is a judgement, not a rule
A split made too early rests on guesses, and wrong boundaries are costly to move
One logical change can now touch several classes if the line was drawn through a single reason to change
whenToUse: A class receives change requests from different teams or stakeholders
A fix for one requirement has broken an unrelated one in the same class
Tests for one concern keep failing because of changes to another
whenNotToUse: A short script or a class that has only ever had one stakeholder: keep it together
To satisfy a rule of one method per class: that is not what the principle asks
Before you have seen any real change requests, when the split would be a guess
pitfalls: Reading it as one method per class, which gives dozens of classes that each change for the same reason
Splitting until nothing can be followed: 40 tiny classes for a 3-step job, where every change edits several of them
Judging by the number of things a class does instead of the number of actors who ask for change
A class that serves finance and operations, so a change for one breaks the other
Splitting by technical step (a class per rule, per rate table, per formatter, per file helper) when one actor's business rules are the real axis of change
Splitting before any change request has shown where the real boundary is, then living with a wrong guess

quiz.question: A teammate says a class breaks the Single Responsibility Principle because it has 12 methods. What is the better question to ask?
options: Whether the class could be split into 12 classes with one method each.
Whether the different methods are all called by the same caller in one place.
How many different groups of people could ask for this class to be changed.
Whether every method name in the class starts with the same verb.
quiz.explanation: The principle counts reasons to change, meaning the actors whose needs drive edits. A class with many methods that all change for one actor is fine, and a class with two methods that serve two teams is not. One method per class is a misreading.

quiz.question: A 3-step report job is split into 40 small classes. One tax-rate change now edits six of them. What does that show?
options: The tax rule was too complicated to split in the first place.
The split went past the actors: one reason to change is spread over many classes.
The principle works, because each class still does exactly one thing.
The tests were badly written and should cover the six classes together.
quiz.explanation: When one request edits many classes, the line was drawn through a single reason to change. The classes each do one small thing but share one reason to change, so they belong together. Following the flow also costs reading time.

quiz.question: Finance and operations both use one report class. Finance changes a tax rule and the report layout breaks. What is the most direct fix that follows the principle?
options: Separate the tax calculation from the layout code, so each team's changes land in its own module.
Add a test for the layout and keep both concerns in the class.
Move the tax rule into a configuration file that only finance can edit.
Ask finance to coordinate every change with operations before merging.
quiz.explanation: The two teams are two reasons to change, so their code belongs in separate modules. Extra tests and coordination treat the symptom, and moving the rule to configuration may still leave layout code next to it.
